question: Civil protection must fulfil the task of responding to wildfires, floods, earthquakes and major industrial and technological accidents with a view to protecting lives and the health of the population, while still facing huge problems and major shortages.

This year’s fire season finds our country in exactly the same situation it found itself in last year, in other words, with a shortage of 4 000 firefighters, with staff being moved around to fill gaps, a tottering forest administration, just 500 foresters when 1 500 more are needed, and no forestry workers. In view of this: 1.

What does the Commission have to say about the fact that rescEU legitimises and perpetuates staff shortages in all Member States while its wholly insufficient fleet is recycled between countries and is usually deployed too late or when a wildfire has already spread uncontrollably?

What does it have to say about the fact that the policy of the EU and of the Greek Government involves devolving ever greater responsibility to volunteer firemen and NGOs, which essentially translates into individual responsibility, rather than providing for permanent staff who are guaranteed full rights in every Member State, full labour rights and paid overtime?

What does it have to say about the fact that the EU refuses to compensate victims of natural disasters because under the conditions of the Recovery and Resilience Facility private losses do not qualify for aid whereas ‘green’ investments for business groups – including in burnt areas or Natura 2000 sites – are considered fully ‘eligible’ and receive generous funding and fast-track authorisation?
answer: Regarding the organisation and functioning of firefighting services, the Commission refers to the reply to written question 000020/2024 of 28 February 2024 (1). The Commission's own capacity rescEU (2) acts as an extra layer of protection for citizens in Europe.

This extra layer aims to boost capacities to respond to disasters such as wildfires, medical emergencies, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear accidents, and to provide shelters, emergency transportation and energy supplies. It has proven successful in providing crucial assistance to countries in need.

Firefighting assets under rescEU are prepositioned in fire prone countries during the summer months to increase the efficiency of the response. Its deployment time depends on several factors, including whether the affected country has requested assistance through the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (3). The EU has only a supporting competence in the area of civil protection.
The exclusive competence for civil protection, including the organisation, functioning and employment conditions of firefighting services, lies within individual Member States.

The EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF) can be activated at the request of a Member State within 12 weeks as from the first damage occurred, demonstrating that the total direct damage exceeds the thresholds specified in Article 2 of Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002 (4). The EUSF may cover part of the costs for emergency and recovery operations incurred by public authorities.
This includes, for example, the recovery of essential infrastructure, provision of temporary accommodation to the population, cleaning-up operations and protection of cultural heritage.
